source_text: THESIS I. DE necessitate gratiae, & de viribus liberi arbitrii, in natura hominis per peccatum corrupta, circa bonum morale, magna est in Schola Romana sententiarum varietas. Ad cujus intelligentiam observandum est in Scholis bonum morale aliquando latius, aliquando strictius sumi. Bonum morale late sumptum significat omne illud quod sic a voluntate & ratione pendet, & utramque afficit, ut propterea homini praemium, vel laus aliqua debeatur, & ejus respectu homo simpliciter bonus denominari possit. Adeoque bonum illud totum situm est in virtute & actionibus secundum virtutem, sive virtus illa sit acquisita, sive infusa, sive ordinis naturalis, sive ordinis supernaturalis.
english: On the necessity of grace and the strength of free choice in human nature corrupted by sin, with respect to moral good, opinions in the Roman School vary widely. To understand this variety we must note that the Schools use 'moral good' sometimes in a wider and sometimes in a stricter sense.

In the wider sense, moral good is everything that depends on will and reason and shapes them both in such a way that a man is owed praise or reward for it and can be called good without qualification. So that good lies entirely in virtue and in acts done according to virtue, whether the virtue is acquired or infused, natural or supernatural.

source_text: II. Hujus boni oppositum est malum illud quod poenam & vituperium meretur, quod malum culpae solet appellari, & sub se omnia vitia & peccata comprehendit. Ab hoc vero bono contradistinguitur bonum quod dicitur Physicum, seu naturae, quod scilicet, a nostra voluntate non pendet, & naturam ita perficit, ut non propterea laus, vel praemium quoddam nobis debeatur, nec ab eo simpliciter boni denominemur.
english: Its opposite is the evil that deserves punishment and blame. This is usually called the evil of fault, and it includes all vices and sins.

Set against this good is the good called physical, or the good of nature. It does not depend on our will, and it perfects our nature without earning us any praise or reward; it does not make us good without qualification.

source_text: III. Ad bonum autem istud quod Physicum dicitur, pertinet tum natura ipsa, & ejus facultates, tum commoda & dona quaecunque illam extra rationem virtutis perficiunt, cujuscunque tandem generis sint, sive ex principiis naturae oriantur, sive supra naturam a Deo concedantur. Ac propterea hoc bonum non dicitur bonum Physicum, seu naturae, ut per id opponatur bono supernaturali, sed solum ut opponatur bono morali, quod modo descriptum est.
english: Physical good includes nature itself and its faculties, and every advantage and gift that perfects nature apart from the character of virtue, of whatever kind, whether it springs from natural principles or is granted by God above nature.
So this good is called physical, or the good of nature, not to set it against supernatural good, but only to set it against moral good as just described.

source_text: IV. Hoc sensu bonum morale a Protestantibus frequenter usurpatur, ut praesertim videre est in thesibus Salmuriensibus. In hac vero disputatione Scholae Romanae Theologi bonum morale paulo strictius sumunt. Nam bonum morale opponunt non tantum bono naturae seu Physico, sed etiam bono supernaturali. Adeoque sub bono morali non comprehendunt virtutes Theologicas, sive infusas, & actus inde promanantes qui sunt ordinis supernaturalis; sed solum omne illud quod rectae rationi & legi naturae conforme est, & tamen supra naturam non assurgit. Ac proinde totum illud bonum positum est in observatione legis illius, quae naturaliter cordi hominis est inscripta, quam Deus in Decalogo summatim comprehendit, & quae non est aliud quam rectae rationis dictamen.
english: Protestants often use 'moral good' in this sense, as can be seen above all in the Saumur theses. In this dispute, however, the theologians of the Roman School take it a little more strictly. They set moral good not only against the good of nature, or physical good, but also against supernatural good.

So they do not include under moral good the theological or infused virtues and the acts that flow from them, which belong to the supernatural order. They include only what agrees with right reason and the law of nature without rising above nature. On their view the whole of that good consists in keeping the law written by nature on the human heart, which God summed up in the Decalogue and which is nothing other than the dictate of right reason.

source_text: V. Porro legis istius praecepta duplici modo observari possunt. Primo duntaxat secundum operum substantiam. Secundo quoad modum quo ordinantur ad salutem aeternam & beatitudinem nobis promissam. Quoad operis substantiam praeceptum legis servat, qui voluntarie abstinet ab eo quod aliquo legis praecepto prohibetur, verbi causa, a furto, & ab homicidio, & qui voluntarie praestat aliquid quod lege jubetur, ut est honorem parenti exhibere, curam gerere suorum, & egenti de suo subvenire. Sed ut ista nobis prosint ad salutem aeternam, requiritur praeterea ut fiant ex charitate, & ex illo Dei amore quem commendat Evangelium, ac ut ad Dei gloriam dirigantur. Adeoque legis praecepta servare posteriori isto modo, est non solum opus quod lege praecipitur, sive externum sit, sive internum etiam, praestare, sed praeterea istud ex charitate facere.
english: The precepts of that law can be kept in two ways: first, only as to the substance of the works; second, in the manner by which they are ordered to eternal salvation and the blessedness promised to us.

A man keeps a precept as to the substance of the work when he freely refrains from what a precept forbids, such as theft or murder, or freely does what the law commands, such as honouring a parent, caring for his own family, or helping the needy from his own means.

For such works to profit us toward eternal salvation, more is needed: they must be done out of charity, from the love of God that the Gospel commends, and directed to God's glory. So to keep the precepts in this second way is not only to do the work the law commands, outward or inward, but also to do it out of charity.

source_text: VI. Rursus observant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae illos qui legis praecepta quoad operum substantiam observant, nec tamen istud ex charitate praestant, in duplici adhuc esse differentia. Potest enim, inquiunt, legis aliquod praeceptum servari quoad substantiam operis, etiam cum peccato, & ita ut actio laudabilis vel honesta censeri non debeat. Quum scilicet, aliquis agit ex prava cupiditate, & in malum aliquem finem, ut si quis depositum amico restituat, & largiatur aliquid egenti, sed in gratiam meretricis, & ut affectui impudico serviat. Sed quamvis aliquis Dei charitate non ducatur, potest aliquod praeceptum quoad substantiam operis servare, non ex prava cupiditate, sed ex affectu naturali non malo, & finem malum non intendens: seu quia existimat id esse sui officii, & rationi congruum: ita ut in eo novum peccatum non incurrat, sed opus quod ab eo praestatur, moralem quandam honestatem habeat. Ac in ejusmodi mandatorum legis observatione consistit illud bonum quod Scholastici morale appellant, & opponunt bono non tantum naturali, sed etiam supernaturali.
english: The doctors of the Roman Church further observe that those who keep the precepts as to the substance of the works, but not out of charity, still fall into two classes.

'A precept of the law,' they say, 'can be kept as to the substance of the work and still be kept with sin, so that the act should not be counted praiseworthy or honourable. This happens when someone acts from a corrupt desire and for a bad end: for instance, if he returns a deposit to a friend or gives something to the needy, but to please a harlot and serve an unchaste passion.

But a man who is not moved by the love of God can still keep a precept as to the substance of the work, not from corrupt desire but from a natural affection that is not evil, and without aiming at a bad end, because he thinks it his duty and agreeable to reason. Then he commits no new sin in doing it, and the work he does has a certain moral honesty.' The good the Schoolmen call moral consists in keeping the commandments in this way, and they set it against both natural and supernatural good.

source_text: VII. Porro Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae communi consensu agnoscunt neminem absque specialis gratiae auxilio posse praecepta divina observare, vel in totum, vel in parte, quoad modum illum quo ad vitam & salutem aeternam ordinantur: nempe, ita ut observatio ista sit aliquid quod ejus salutem per se promoveat, & gratiam vel gloriam ipsi promereatur.
english: The doctors of the Roman Church agree that without the help of special grace no one can keep God's precepts, wholly or in part, in the way that orders them to life and eternal salvation. That is, no one can keep them so that the keeping of itself advances his salvation and merits grace or glory for him.

source_text: VIII. Nullus quoque eorum negat gratia opus non esse, ut quaedam legis praecepta quoad operis substantiam serventur: sed ita tamen ut actio moraliter bona & honesta non sit, ut quae ex malo fine, & cupiditate prava vitietur. Quod per se notum & manifestum est.
english: None of them denies, either, that some precepts can be kept as to the substance of the work without grace, but only so that the act is not morally good and honourable, being spoiled by a bad end and corrupt desire. That is obvious in itself.

source_text: IX. Verum inter eos quaeritur An absque speciali gratia, & solo generalis auxilii beneficio, sic possint praecepta divina servari, ut quamvis istud ex charitate non fiat, nec sit aeternae vitae meritorium, in eo tamen peccatum vitetur, & actio sit bona & honesta moraliter? Super qua re variae sunt & discrepantes eorum sententiae.
english: The question among them is this: can God's precepts be kept without special grace, by the general help alone, in such a way that, although the act is not done out of charity and does not merit eternal life, sin is still avoided and the act is morally good and honourable? On this their opinions differ widely.

source_text: X. Et primo quidem multi ex veteribus Scholasticis pertendunt hominem in statu naturae corruptae posse propriis viribus, absque specialis gratiae auxilio, omnia & singula legis naturae praecepta servare quoad operum substantiam, & sic totum quod vocant morale bonum efficere. Haec est sententia Durandi in secundum sententiarum, distinctione vigesima octava, quaestione quarta. Ubi affirmat & aliquot argumentis probare contendit, aliquem sine gratia implere posse divina praecepta, quae, scilicet, sunt juris naturalis, non autem supernaturalis. Adeoque concedit fieri posse, ut absque gratia aliquis omni peccato careat, tam omissionis, quam commissionis, licet in eo maneat peccatum originale, propter quod foret salute excludendus.
english: First, many of the older Schoolmen maintain that man in the state of corrupt nature can, by his own strength and without the help of special grace, keep each and every precept of the law of nature as to the substance of the works, and so achieve the whole of what they call moral good.

This is the view of Durandus on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 28, question 4. There he affirms, and tries to prove with several arguments, that a man without grace can fulfil God's precepts, those of natural law though not those of supernatural law. So he grants that someone might, without grace, be free of every sin of omission and of commission, though original sin would remain in him and would shut him out of salvation.

source_text: XI. Postquam enim sic contra propriam sententiam argumentatus est, Nullus damnatur nisi pro peccato commissionis, vel omissionis: sed qui praecepta legis implet, nihil omittit: qui autem omne malum vitat, nihil committit: si igitur sine gratia praecepta legis homo possit implere, cum sine gratia possit peccatum vitare, tunc sine gratia posset homo vitare damnationem: sed qui non damnatur est in gloria: Ergo homo non habens gratiam posset in gloria esse. Respondet, quod absque peccato omissionis & commissionis damnaretur homo pro solo peccato originali, nisi per gratiam liberaretur.
english: He first argues against his own view: 'No one is damned except for a sin of commission or omission. Whoever fulfils the precepts of the law omits nothing, and whoever avoids all evil commits nothing. So if man could fulfil the precepts without grace, he could avoid sin without grace, and so avoid damnation without grace. But whoever is not damned is in glory. So a man without grace could be in glory.'
His answer is that, even without any sin of omission or commission, man would be damned for original sin alone unless grace set him free.

source_text: XII. Pertendit quidem Vasques Durandum ibi loqui, non de gratia quavis, sed solum de gratia habituali & justificante; & non putat aliquem esse Doctorem Catholicum qui docuerit hominem posse evitare omnem tentationem contra jus naturale, ac proinde servare omnem naturalem legem, non solum brevi, sed etiam longo tempore, sine ullo auxilio gratiae per Christum. Durandum enim & alios veteres Scholasticos, quum disputant de victoria tentationum, & de observatione praeceptorum naturalium, An sine gratia possit quis vincere omnes tentationes, & observare omnia praecepta; per gratiam non intelligere auxilium gratiae moventis, sed gratiam habitualem, qua justi sumus. In primam 2. tom. 2. Disput. 189. cap. 2.
english: Vázquez does maintain that Durandus is speaking there not of any grace at all but only of habitual and justifying grace. He does not think any Catholic doctor has taught that man can resist every temptation against natural law, and so keep the whole natural law, not only for a short time but for a long time too, without any help of grace through Christ.

When Durandus and the other older Schoolmen debate the overcoming of temptations and the keeping of the natural precepts, and ask whether a man can overcome all temptations and keep all the precepts without grace, by 'grace' they mean, he says, not the help of moving grace but habitual grace, by which we are righteous. On the Prima Secundae, vol. 2, disputation 189, chapter 2.

source_text: XIII. Sed legenti & expendenti Durandum patet Vasquem in eo falli, & mentem Durandi esse, hominem per naturae vires, & absque auxilio quocunque gratiae per Christum implere posse divina praecepta. Etenim sententiam suam probat hoc argumento. Illud quod homo naturaliter facit, sine gratia per seipsum facere potest: sed gentes quae legem non habent, naturaliter quae legis sunt faciunt, ut dicitur, Rom. 2. Ergo praecepta legis sine gratia impleri possunt. Unde patet Durando idem esse sine gratia facere, quod naturaliter & per seipsum facere. Qui autem aliquid facit mediante aliquo gratiae per Christum auxilio, illud dici non potest naturaliter & per seipsum facere, etiamsi alioqui gratia habituali & justificante careat. Adde quod Durandus ad eandem distinctionem scribens quaestione secunda, objicit sibi illa Christi verba, sine me nihil potestis facere. Ad quae respondet verba ista intelligenda esse de generali influentia Dei, qua rerum principia in esse conservat, sine qua nihil esset, aut fieret.
english: Anyone who reads Durandus carefully can see that Vázquez is wrong here. Durandus means that man, by the strength of nature and without any help of grace through Christ, can fulfil God's precepts. He proves his view with this argument: 'What man does naturally he can do of himself without grace. But the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, as Romans 2 says. So the precepts of the law can be fulfilled without grace.'

So for Durandus to act without grace is the same as to act naturally and of oneself. But a man who does something through some help of grace from Christ cannot be said to do it naturally and of himself, even if he lacks habitual and justifying grace.

Besides, in question 2 of the same distinction Durandus raises against himself Christ's words, 'Without me you can do nothing.' He replies that they must be understood of God's general influence, by which he keeps the principles of things in being, and without which nothing would exist or happen.

source_text: XIV. Eandem vero cum Durando sententiam amplexi sunt Scotus & Gabriel Biel. Opinantur enim cum illo, hominem, etiam peccato corruptum, posse omnia praecepta moralia, seu legis naturae, secundum substantiam operum, servare per vires suas, sine gratia, licet non in ordine ad finem supernaturalem: ut testatur Estius in secundum sententiarum, Distinctione vigesima sexta paragrapho quadragesimo propositione octava. Verum haec sententia in Schola Romana communiter hodie rejicitur. Atque Estii judicio manifestum est illam ad Pelagii haeresin spectare, & contrariam ad fidem Catholicam.
english: Scotus and Gabriel Biel took the same view as Durandus. With him they hold that man, even corrupted by sin, can by his own strength and without grace keep all the moral precepts, the precepts of the law of nature, as to the substance of the works, though not as ordered to the supernatural end. So Estius reports on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 40, proposition 8.
But the Roman School today commonly rejects this view, and in Estius's judgement it plainly leans toward the heresy of Pelagius and is contrary to the Catholic faith.

source_text: XV. Verum in Schola Romana, non tantum olim reperti sunt, sed etiam hodie quoque reperiuntur, qui fatentur quidem non posse servari omnia praecepta, & vinci omnem tentationem universim, & ut dici solet, collective ab homine in statu, quem modo habet: sed tamen posse sigillatim, sine ullo auxilio gratiae per Christum, servari quodlibet praeceptum naturale, quantumvis difficile, & vinci quamlibet tentationem quantumvis vehementem. Hanc sententiam Vasquez Disputationis modo citatae capite secundo tribuit Ruardo Tappero Theologo Lovaniensi ad articulum septimum Academiae Lovaniensis, Paragr. Haec confirmantur. Et certe ibi doctor ille loquens de operibus quae ex suo genere naturae nostrae vires non excedunt, qualia sunt omnia quae naturali lege praecipiuntur, dicit haec singula, quamvis simus infirmi, & gratia destituti, in nostra esse potestate. Nemo enim est, inquit, qui non potest nolle, & etiam vitare homicidium, & quodlibet aliud peccatum etiam veniale. Nam nulla passio, nulla mortis formido inducere potest necessitatem ipsam sequendi, ut non maneat in nostra potestate ipsum velle & nolle, quamdiu non absorbetur, sed liberum manet judicium rationis. Quibus statim subjungit, Necessitas igitur peccandi quae ex nostra est infirmitate, opponitur inevitabilitati quoad universa, non quoad singula, nec est ad aliquod peccatum in specie committendum. Eandem vero sententiam a quibusdam recentioribus suo tempore retentam fuisse testatur Vasques jam supra citata disputatione capite secundo. Additque viginti ante annis illam non parum fuisse in Hispania communem.
english: Some in the Roman School, in the past and still today, admit that man in his present state cannot keep all the precepts and overcome every temptation taken all together, or, as they say, collectively. Yet they hold that, one by one and without any help of grace through Christ, he can keep any natural precept, however hard, and overcome any temptation, however strong.

In chapter 2 of the disputation just cited, Vázquez ascribes this view to Ruard Tapper, the Louvain theologian, on the seventh article of the Academy of Louvain, at the paragraph 'Haec confirmantur'. And there that doctor does say of works that by their kind do not exceed the strength of our nature, as is true of everything the natural law commands, that each of them is in our power, weak and without grace though we are.

'There is no one,' he says, 'who cannot refuse, and even avoid, murder or any other sin, even venial. No passion and no fear of death can make it necessary to follow it in such a way that willing and refusing do not stay in our power, so long as reason is not overwhelmed and its judgement stays free.' He adds at once: 'So the necessity of sinning that comes from our weakness is set against inevitability as to all sins together, not as to each; nor is it a necessity of committing any particular sin.'
Vázquez reports, in the disputation cited above, chapter 2, that some more recent writers of his time held the same view, and adds that twenty years earlier it was quite common in Spain.

source_text: XVI. Sed in Schola Romana longe communior est tertia quaedam sententia. Illa statuit hominem in statu corruptionis, absque speciali gratiae divinae auxilio, servare non posse legis naturalis praecepta, nec omnia collective, nec etiam singula seorsim: quoniam inter illa sunt quae vires naturae corruptae superant: quale est praeceptum de non concupiscendo, & illud quo jubemur Deum ut authorem naturae ex toto corde diligere. Imo urgente gravi tentatione, qui sunt in hac sententia fatentur, nullum mandatum legis moralis impleri, nec ullum morale bonum perfici posse. Sed quum nulla gravis tentatio occurrit, pertendunt cum solo Dei concursu generali, & absque peculiari gratiae auxilio, opera legis moralis faciliora sic, quoad substantiam operis, servari posse, ut omne novum peccatum vitetur. Exempli causa, aliquem nulla interiori gratia a Deo praeventum, posse parentibus honorem exhibere, egenti subvenire, interrogatum vera respondere, depositum amico reddere; non ex prava cupiditate, quo in casu actiones illae vitio non carerent, sed ex naturali quadam propensione non mala: nec etiam in malum aliquem finem, sed simpliciter quia id judicat rationi consentaneum, & ad officium suum pertinere. Quo posito, existimant ejusmodi actionem nullum peccatum in se includere, sed revera moraliter bonam & honestam esse, quanquam ad salutem aeternam nihil prosit: nec sit gratiae, vel gloriae ullo modo meritoria.
english: Far more common in the Roman School is a third view. It holds that man in the state of corruption cannot, without the special help of divine grace, keep the precepts of the natural law, either all together or even one by one, because some of them exceed the strength of corrupt nature: such as the precept against coveting, and the command to love God as the author of nature with all our heart. Those who hold this view admit that under grave temptation no commandment of the moral law can be fulfilled and no moral good achieved.

But when no grave temptation arises, they maintain that with God's general concurrence alone, without any particular help of grace, the easier works of the moral law can be kept as to the substance of the work in such a way that every new sin is avoided.

For example, a man not moved beforehand by any inward grace from God can honour his parents, help the needy, answer truthfully when asked, and return a deposit to a friend. He does it not from corrupt desire, for then the acts would be vicious, but from a natural inclination that is not evil; and not for a bad end, but simply because he judges it reasonable and part of his duty. On that basis they hold that such an act contains no sin and is truly morally good and honourable, though it does nothing for eternal salvation and merits neither grace nor glory in any way.

source_text: XVII. Hanc sententiam late tuentur & explicant Bellarminus & Estius cum plurimis aliis, qui tamen, licet fateantur quaedam legis moralis praecepta difficiliora sine gratia servari non posse, concedunt nihilominus hominem in statu naturae corruptae, ad aliquod breve tempus posse sine gratia servare omnia praecepta legis naturae, quae servanda per idem tempus occurrunt: Quoniam, ut aiunt, praecepta legis affirmativa non obligant ad semper, nec omnia occurrunt simul implenda: praecepta vero negativa servantur etiam nihil agendo, ut illud, Non occides. Potest autem homo ad tempus aliquod, quoad hujusmodi praecepta, negative se habere, nulla in contrarium occurrente tentatione. Ut videre est apud Estium in 2. sentent. distinct. 26. paragr. 40.
english: Bellarmine and Estius, with very many others, defend and explain this view at length. They admit that some of the harder precepts of the moral law cannot be kept without grace. Yet they grant that man in the state of corrupt nature can, for a short time, keep without grace all the precepts of the law of nature that fall to be kept in that time.

Their reason is this: the affirmative precepts do not bind at every moment, and they do not all arise to be fulfilled at once; and the negative precepts, such as 'You shall not kill', are kept even by doing nothing. For a time, then, a man can hold back with respect to such precepts, if no temptation to the contrary arises. See Estius on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 40.

source_text: XVIII. Quibus similia apud Bellarminum quoque leguntur. Explicans enim quo sensu negaverat, solis naturae viribus servari posse omnia praecepta moralia secundum substantiam operis, significare non volumus, inquit, non posse aliquem ad brevissimum tempus omnia servare: cum possit fieri, ut aliquando nullum occurrat praeceptum affirmativum, & nulla adsit tentatio provocans ad violanda praecepta negativa. Itaque sententia propositionis illius haec est, ut non possint longiore aliquo tempore, quo varia praecepta observanda se offerunt, solis naturae viribus, ita omnia adimpleri, ut omni ex parte peccatum vitetur. De gratia & libero arbitrio lib. 5. cap. 5.
english: Bellarmine says much the same. Explaining in what sense he had denied that all the moral precepts can be kept as to the substance of the work by the strength of nature alone, he writes: 'We do not mean that no one can keep them all for a very short time. It can happen that for a while no affirmative precept arises and no temptation urges us to break the negative ones.

So the sense of the proposition is that over any longer time, in which various precepts present themselves to be kept, they cannot all be fulfilled by the strength of nature alone in such a way that sin is wholly avoided.' De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 5, chapter 5.

source_text: XIX. Attamen in Schola Romana reperiuntur non pauci qui affirmant nullum opus morale ex omni circumstantia bonum posse fieri sine auxilio gratiae. Haec est sententia Gabrielis Vasques in primam secundae tomo secundo disputatione centesima & nonagesima. Ubi pro se plurimos citat ex Scholasticis, tam veteribus quam recentioribus, Et inter alios Alphonsum a Castro, qui hanc assertionem ut Catholicam ponit, Liberum hominis arbitrium ex sola sua potestate, addita etiam illa communi & generali Dei concausatione, non potest sine aliquo Dei speciali auxilio bonum aliquod operari, quoniam semper circa illud praecedit quaedam monitio, aut attractio, aut inspiratio, aut aliquod donum naturae superadditum, quod ipse Deus mere gratis, quibus illi placet, donat. Libro septimo adversus haereses. Verbo Gratia: haeresi 1. assertione 3.
english: Yet not a few in the Roman School affirm that no moral work good in every circumstance can be done without the help of grace. This is Gabriel Vázquez's view on the Prima Secundae, vol. 2, disputation 190. There he cites very many Schoolmen, older and more recent, on his side.

Among them is Alfonso de Castro, who lays down as Catholic the assertion: 'Man's free choice, by its own power alone, even with God's common and general co-causation added, cannot do any good without some special help from God. For every such good is always preceded by some warning, drawing, inspiration, or some gift added over and above nature, which God himself gives purely as a gift to whom he pleases.' Adversus haereses, book 7, under 'Grace', heresy 1, assertion 3.

source_text: XX. Quibus consentanea docet Joannes Roffensis in Anglia Episcopus. Patrum, inquit, sententiam sequi malui quam Scholasticorum, cum in hac re mutuo sibi pugnent. Patres enim asserunt neminem quicquam posse boni velle sine Dei speciali auxilio, nec sufficere generalem illum influxum. Nonnulli contra Scholastici sic contendunt, hunc sufficere, ut quis absque illo auxilio bene moraliter agere, & bonum facere possit, non solum ex genere, verum etiam quod debitis undique circumstantiis ornatum sit. Articulo 36. adversus Lutherum. paragr. Neutrum sane potest.
english: John Fisher, bishop of Rochester in England, teaches the same. 'I have preferred,' he says, 'to follow the Fathers rather than the Schoolmen, since on this matter they contradict each other. The Fathers assert that no one can will anything good without God's special help, and that the general influence is not enough.

Some Schoolmen, on the other hand, contend that it is enough: that without that help a man can act morally well and do good, not only good in kind but also good furnished on every side with the proper circumstances.' Against Luther, article 36, at the paragraph 'Neutrum sane potest'.

source_text: XXI. Igitur ex horum Doctorum sententia, homo in statu peccati absque Dei gratia nihil operari potest quod vere sit virtutis opus, quodque simpliciter bonum & honestum dici mereatur: quoniam in eo statu, quaecunque opera ab homine fiunt, ut ut speciosa sint, & extrinsecus honesta videantur, ex circumstantiae alicujus defectu vitiosa redduntur, & quandam peccati rationem contrahunt. Quae gratia autem sit necessaria ad hoc, ut homo corruptus bene operari possit & verum legi morali obsequium praestare, studiose explicat Vasques modo citata disputatione. Etenim initio capitis primi monet quaestionem hic non esse, An gratia habitualis & gratum faciens atque justificans, quae juxta ipsum in charitate consistit, necessaria sit ad hoc, ut quis secundum legem moralem bene operetur. Neque etiam quaeri utrum omnia opera ejus qui in peccato est, peccata sint. Imo neque an fides necessaria sit ad bene operandum, sed solum an sine quodam gratiae auxilio homo possit secundum virtutem operari. Caeterum, inquit, in hac controversia quaestio nobis futura non est, an infidelis aliqua bona facere possit; neque disputandum erit, an sine charitate aliquod bonum fieri queat; neque utrum omnia opera existentis in peccato peccata sint, an aliqua bona ille efficere possit: sed controversia nunc est, an sine auxilio gratiae Dei possit homo aliquod bonum opus, secundum virtutem, operari; quae sane quaestio longe diversa est.
english: On these doctors' view, then, man in the state of sin can do nothing without God's grace that is truly a work of virtue and deserves to be called good and honourable without qualification. In that state, whatever works a man does, however fine and outwardly honourable they look, are made vicious by the lack of some circumstance and take on something of the character of sin.

What grace is needed for corrupt man to act well and give true obedience to the moral law, Vázquez explains carefully in the disputation just cited. At the start of chapter 1 he points out that the question is not whether habitual grace, the grace that makes acceptable and justifies, which he places in charity, is needed for acting well by the moral law. Nor is it whether all the works of a man in sin are sins, nor even whether faith is needed to act well; it is only whether man can act virtuously without some help of grace.

'In this controversy,' he says, 'our question will not be whether an unbeliever can do some good things. We will not dispute whether some good can be done without charity, or whether all the works of a man in sin are sins or he can do some good ones. The controversy now is whether man can do any good work according to virtue without the help of God's grace; and that is a very different question.'

source_text: XXII. Concedit igitur ille nec charitatem quam Spiritus Sanctus in fidelium corda diffundit, nec ipsam fidem necessariam esse, ad hoc ut aliquis bene operetur, & legi morali atque naturali veram exhibeat obedientiam; sed ab homine non tantum in peccato jacente, verum etiam adhuc infideli, posse opus aliquod moraliter bonum procedere. Hoc solum negat hominem peccatorem, & omni gratiae divinae auxilio destitutum, posse bene agere, & secundum virtutem & honestatem naturalem.
english: So he grants that neither the charity the Holy Spirit pours into the hearts of believers nor faith itself is needed for someone to act well and give true obedience to the moral and natural law. A morally good work can come from a man who is not only lying in sin but is still an unbeliever.
The one thing he denies is that a sinner, without any help of divine grace at all, can act well, even by the standard of natural virtue and honesty.

source_text: XXIII. Quae sit autem illa gratia quam ad hoc necessario requiri existimat, fusius explicat ipse ejusdem disputationis capite duodecimo. Ubi duplex auxilium gratiae per Christum distinguit, unum quod suapte natura sit ordinis supernaturalis, alterum quod sit ordinis naturalis. Et prius quidem illud necessarium non putat ad quodlibet opus virtutis moralis, sed solum posterius, quod est ordinis naturalis. Ejus enim sententia est, posse quidem hominem singula opera moralis virtutis efficere sine auxilio gratiae per Christum, quod suapte natura sit ordinis supernaturalis, quale ad opera virtutum infusarum necessarium est; non tamen posse ullum opus morale secundum virtutem ex omni parte bonum operari, sine aliquo auxilio gratiae per Christum, quod suapte natura ordinis naturalis sit, & per causas naturales aeterna Dei misericordia nobis praeparetur.
english: What that necessary grace is, he explains more fully in chapter 12 of the same disputation. There he distinguishes two helps of grace through Christ: one supernatural by its own nature, the other natural. He does not think the first is needed for any work of moral virtue; only the second is, which belongs to the natural order.

His view is that man can do particular works of moral virtue without the help of grace through Christ that is supernatural by nature, the kind needed for the works of the infused virtues. But he cannot do any moral work that is virtuous and good in every respect without some help of grace through Christ that is natural by nature and is prepared for us through natural causes by God's eternal mercy.

source_text: XXIV. Quanquam autem istud auxilium juxta ipsum sit ordinis naturalis, affirmat tamen illud distinctum esse a dono creationis, & communi influxu, quo Deus cum omnibus causis naturalibus concurrit. Illud vero praecipue constituit in sancta quadam cogitatione, qua nos a Deo praeveniri ad singula bona opera necessarium existimat. Nam necessitatem gratiae ad singula bona opera probat ex praeparatione cogitationis, qua praevenimur per opera singula. Nam, inquit, quamvis simus liberi arbitrii, & voluntas nostra libere feratur in utramque partem; tamen quia sine cogitatione moveri nulla ratione potest, & ab extrinseco principio ad hanc primam cogitationem, potius quam ad oppositam applicari debet; efficitur ut quoties cogitatione ad bonum excitatur, cum posset non excitari, gratiam peculiarem a Deo recipiat distinctam a gratia & dono creationis. Quoniam cum liberum esset Deo non admovere nos ad hanc & illam boni cogitationem, peculiare in hoc nobis beneficium confert: sive haec applicatio fit proxime ab ipso Deo, sive per causas alias extrinsecas. Nam quocunque modo fiat, tandem ad Deum referenda est: eo quod omnes causae ad hanc cogitationem excitandam ita ordinatae sunt divina providentia, & praescientia, ut contrariae possent ordinari, vel ipsae aliter disponi. Itaque ad hanc cogitationem boni, liberali Dei voluntate nobis praeparatam, reducit peculiarem gratiam Dei, qua omnia opera bona etiam moralia efficimus.
english: Although on his view this help belongs to the natural order, he affirms that it is distinct from the gift of creation and from the common influence by which God concurs with all natural causes. He places it chiefly in a holy thought by which, he holds, God must go before us for each good work. He proves that grace is needed for each good work from the thought prepared for us beforehand for each one.

'Although we have free choice,' he says, 'and our will moves freely either way, it cannot be moved at all without a thought, and something outside it must bring it to this first thought rather than the opposite one. So whenever it is stirred to good by a thought, when it might not have been, it receives from God a particular grace distinct from the grace and gift of creation.

Since God was free not to bring us to this or that good thought, he does us a particular kindness in it, whether he applies it directly himself or through other outside causes. However it happens, it must finally be traced to God, because divine providence and foreknowledge so order all the causes that stir this thought that contrary causes could have been ordered, or these arranged otherwise.' So he traces to this good thought, prepared for us by God's free will, the particular grace of God by which we do all good works, moral ones included.

source_text: XXV. Statuit ergo Doctor ille non omnem Sanctam cogitationem vel esse fidem ipsam, vel incipere post fidem, aut a fide: sed vult sanctas cogitationes hominibus a Deo inspirari per causas naturales, etiam antequam credant & fidem concipiant. Et nihilominus observat hoc genus auxilii quod est ordinis naturalis, quandoquidem consistit in bonis cogitationibus quae naturae lumen non transcendunt, dici posse quodammodo supra naturam nostram, quatenus est supra nostram industriam, & solicitudinem, sine qua Deus nobis talem cogitationem praeparavit, & concessit, cum posset oppositam immittere. Tum etiam quia haec auxilia, quae nobis confert ad recte vivendum quocunque genere virtutis, & ad vincendas tentationes, & concupiscentias, dantur nobis a Deo ex intentione nostrae beatitudinis, quae est finis noster supernaturalis. Tom. 2. in 1. 2. disput. 189. cap. 16.
english: So that doctor holds that not every holy thought either is faith itself or begins after faith or from it. He maintains that God inspires holy thoughts in men through natural causes even before they believe and come to faith.

Yet he notes that this kind of help, though it belongs to the natural order, since it consists in good thoughts that do not go beyond the light of nature, can be called in a sense above our nature. It is above our own effort and care: God prepared and granted us such a thought without them, when he could have sent us the opposite one.

It can also be called so because the helps he gives us for living rightly in any kind of virtue, and for overcoming temptations and desires, are given us by God with our blessedness in view, which is our supernatural end. Vol. 2 on the Prima Secundae, disputation 189, chapter 16.

source_text: XXVI. Unde est quod idem auxilium ad quodlibet bonum opus morale necessarium, licet quoad substantiam sit ordinis naturalis, ad gratiam tamen Christi pertinere contendit. Quoniam videlicet opera moraliter bona, quae per tale auxilium fiunt, etiam ab infidelibus, ad justificationem, & consequenter ad aeternam salutem, quodammodo disponunt, & gratiae justificantis sunt impetratoria. Sicut, inquit, Christus mortuus est, ut impii justificarentur, ita etiam ut recte viverent: nam & bonis operibus & recta vita, etiam secundum virtutem moralem, spiritum compunctionis, & justificationis a Deo impetramus. Qua ratione putat sufficienter probari, hoc auxilium gratiae distinctum a dono creationis requisitum ad singula bona opera moralia esse per Christum. Jam citata disputatione 190. cap. 12.
english: That is why he contends that this help, needed for any good moral work, belongs to the grace of Christ, even though in substance it is of the natural order. Morally good works done through such help, even by unbelievers, in some way dispose men to justification and so to eternal salvation, and they serve to obtain justifying grace.

'Christ died,' he says, 'that the ungodly might be justified, and also that they might live rightly. For by good works and an upright life, even in moral virtue, we obtain from God the spirit of compunction and of justification.' By this reasoning he thinks it sufficiently shown that this help of grace, distinct from the gift of creation and required for each good moral work, comes through Christ. Disputation 190 already cited, chapter 12.

source_text: XXVII. Quanquam ergo Doctor ille auxilium aliquod gratiae Christi necessarium putet, ad hoc ut aliquis bene moraliter operetur, nihilominus cum longe maxima Scholae Romanae parte, sentit gratiam illam in eum cadere posse qui fide destitutus est. Neque fidei nomine solum veram fidem in Christum intelligit, sed etiam qualemcunque unius veri Dei cognitionem, cujusmodi reperiri potest, non tantum in haereticis, sed etiam in infidelibus & gentilibus multis. Nam ejus sententia est, in quocunque genere infidelium, etiam gentilium, nec unum verum Deum cognoscentium, posse esse aliqua moralium virtutum opera, & aliquando esse, licet id raro contingat. Disput. 191. cap. 2.
english: So although that doctor thinks some help of the grace of Christ is needed for anyone to act morally well, he holds with by far the largest part of the Roman School that this grace can be given to someone who has no faith. By 'faith' he means not only true faith in Christ but any knowledge at all of the one true God, which can be found not only in heretics but also in many unbelievers and pagans.

His view is that among every kind of unbeliever, even pagans who do not know the one true God, there can be, and sometimes are, works of the moral virtues, though this happens rarely. Disputation 191, chapter 2.

source_text: XXVIII. Quam sententiam amplectitur Estius in secundum sententiarum Distinctione quadragesima prima paragrapho tertio. Ibi enim asserit quasdam infidelium actiones non tantum non esse peccata, sed & moraliter, licet imperfecte, bonas. Et notat hoc in loco a se infidelem non dici Judaeum aut haereticum, tametsi revera talis fidem non habeat, propterea quod fides integrae virtutis sit nomen, sed paganum, seu Ethnicum, qui ne unius quidem Dei, in quem suas actiones referre possit, cognitionem habeat. Censet enim ejusmodi infidelem aliquando operari ex naturali affectu, qui ex se ad bonum tendit, & actiones quasdam non in malum finem dirigere, sed ad bonum & finem ultimum in genere & confuse cognitum; quod sufficit ejus judicio ut non habeant rationem peccati. Nam sicut justi in hac vita non omnes suas actiones in Deum, quem habent pro fine ultimo, referunt, eas nimirum in quibus quotidie offendunt: ita nec necesse putat, ut injusti, licet infideles, referant omnes suas actiones, in illud quod prava voluntate statuerunt sibi summe diligendum. Quemadmodum enim concupiscentia interdum in justis surripit aliquos motus voluntatis, qui non referuntur in Deum, ut finem ultimum, ac ne referri quidem possunt; sic naturalis ad bonum instinctus aliquando, ex ejus mente, in infidelibus elicit actiones quasdam, quas homo non refert ad illud quod in particulari pro summo bono diligit, sed ad bonum & finem ultimum, saltem in genere, licet quis sit ille finis in particulari & distincte ignoretur.
english: Estius takes this view on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 41, paragraph 3. He asserts there that some actions of unbelievers are not only not sins but are morally good, though imperfectly. He notes that by 'unbeliever' he does not mean a Jew or a heretic, even though such a person in truth has no faith, since faith is the name of a whole virtue. He means a pagan or heathen, who has no knowledge even of the one God to whom he might refer his actions.

He thinks such an unbeliever sometimes acts from a natural affection that of itself tends toward good, and directs some actions not to a bad end but to the good and to the last end, known in general and vaguely. In his judgement that is enough for them not to have the character of sin.

The righteous in this life do not refer all their actions to God, whom they hold as their last end; they do not so refer those in which they stumble daily. Likewise, he thinks, the unrighteous, even unbelievers, need not refer all their actions to what their corrupt will has set up as the thing to love above all.

Just as desire sometimes slips into the righteous some movements of the will that are not referred to God as last end, and cannot even be, so, on his view, the natural instinct for good sometimes draws from unbelievers actions that a man does not refer to what he loves in particular as the highest good. He refers them to the good and to the last end, at least in general, though he does not know what that end is in particular and distinctly.

source_text: XXIX. Quibus affine est quod docet Vasquez, nempe ad hoc ut opera nostra sint bona & honesta, debere quidem referri in Deum ut ultimum finem, non tamen voluntate aliqua praecedente, ex qua habitu dicantur referri, sed ex sola natura operis, sine alia motione voluntatis. Adeoque sufficere ad hoc ut infidelis bonum opus faciat, si sciat illud esse bonum & propter ipsam virtutis honestatem illud amet: hoc ipso enim tale opus sufficienter ad Deum referri. Nuper citata Disput. cap. 2. & 3.
english: Close to this is Vázquez's teaching. For our works to be good and honourable, he says, they must indeed be referred to God as last end, but not by some prior act of will by which they could be said to be referred habitually; they are referred by the very nature of the work, without any further movement of the will.

So for an unbeliever to do a good work it is enough that he knows it is good and loves it for the sake of virtue's own honesty; by that very fact the work is sufficiently referred to God. Disputation just cited, chapters 2 and 3.

source_text: XXX. Caeterum ista Gulielmi Estii & Gabrielis Vasquez sententia Pontificum Romanorum calculo comprobatur. Si quidem opposita doctrina damnata esse videtur in Bulla edita a Pio V. & a Gregorio XIII. confirmata. Nam inter alias propositiones quae in ea Bulla damnatae sunt, contra Doctorem quendam Lovaniensem, una est his verbis concepta. Omnia opera infidelium sunt peccata, & Philosophorum virtutes sunt vitia. Ut testatur Vasquez loco jam allegato.
english: The popes of Rome have given their verdict for this view of Estius and Vázquez. The contrary teaching appears to stand condemned in Pius V's bull, which Gregory XIII later confirmed.

That bull, aimed at a Louvain doctor, condemns several propositions, and one of them reads: 'All the works of unbelievers are sins, and the virtues of the philosophers are vices.' Vázquez reports this in the passage cited above.

source_text: XXXI. Reperiuntur tamen in Schola Romana nonnulli, qui contra quod Bulla citata decernitur, affirmant nullum opus infidelium esse moraliter bonum. Idque quoniam ut opus sit secundum virtutem, & moraliter bonum, non solum fieri debet id quod oportet, sed etiam debet fieri quando, & quantum, & cujus gratia oportet. Finis autem cujus gratia omne opus fieri debet, est Deus ab agente dilectus, in quem reliqua referantur: quia cum Deus solus sit propter se diligendus, omnis affectus qui non fertur in Deum tanquam in finem est malus. Unde concludunt nullum opus infidelium bonum esse, propterea quod veri Dei notitiam non habent, ac proinde nullam suam operationem in verum Deum tanquam in finem ultimum referunt.
english: Yet some in the Roman School, against what the bull decrees, affirm that no work of unbelievers is morally good. Their reason is that for a work to be virtuous and morally good, it is not enough to do what ought to be done; it must also be done when, as much as, and for the sake for which it ought to be done.

The end for whose sake every work must be done is God, loved by the one acting, and everything else is referred to him. Since God alone is to be loved for his own sake, every affection not directed to God as its end is evil. So they conclude that no work of unbelievers is good, because they do not know the true God and so refer none of their acts to him as last end.

source_text: XXXII. Hanc sententiam Vasquez, saepius citata disputatione centesima nonagesima prima, tribuit Gregorio Ariminensi, Doctori inter Scholasticos celebri, quem observat per infideles, a quibus nullum bonum opus procedere queat, intelligere eos qui sunt infideles simpliciter, id est, Gentiles qui non habent notitiam unius veri Dei; non autem Schismaticos & Haereticos, eosque ex infidelibus qui aliqua fide credunt & cognoscunt esse unum Deum. Adeoque Doctor ille, ut quis bene operetur, non existimat necessariam esse fidem infusam & supernaturalem, sed quamcunque fidem & cognitionem unius veri Dei. Nec tamen desunt in Schola Romana qui ad operandum bene moraliter, requirant fidem non quamlibet, sed ipsam Christi fidem, quo de numero est Linconiensis quidam, eodem Vasquez referente.
english: Vázquez, in the often-cited disputation 191, ascribes this view to Gregory of Rimini, a celebrated Schoolman. He notes that by the unbelievers from whom no good work can come Gregory means unbelievers in the plain sense, that is, Gentiles who have no knowledge of the one true God. He does not mean schismatics and heretics, or those unbelievers who by some faith believe and know that there is one God.

So for someone to act well, that doctor does not think infused and supernatural faith necessary, only some faith and knowledge of the one true God. Still, there are some in the Roman School who require for acting morally well not just any faith but the faith of Christ itself. Among them, Vázquez again reports, is one 'Lincolniensis'.
